entries.paper_title: Data-driven identification of predictive risk biomarkers for subgroups of osteoarthritis using interpretable machine learning
entries.prediction_task: 5-year osteoarthritis risk prediction

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Models incorporate data gathered over the subsequent five years (or until OA diagnosis), effectively conditioning on future observations. One cannot anticipate factors like NSAID use four years into the future. The study essentially assumes the form of a retrospective study, not a prediction model.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have revised the paper to clarify this is a retrospective characterization study, not a prospective prediction model. The study design section has been rewritten.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: NSAIDs are commonly prescribed for OA management and should preferably not be incorporated into a model designed to predict the onset of OA. NSAID prescriptions up to one year before OA diagnosis as a feature is essentially a proxy for existing disease.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We acknowledge this concern and have added discussion about NSAID as a potential indicator of early-stage disease rather than a predictor.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Prior studies based on UK Biobank have demonstrated that models solely incorporating age, sex, and BMI can predict OA with AUC of 0.685-0.701. It is essential to compare the authors' models with simpler models incorporating established risk factors.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added comparison with a baseline model using age, sex, and BMI only.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Inclusion of highly correlated variables (e.g., fat mass ratios in right leg vs left leg, grip strength right vs left hand) should be reconsidered to avoid multicollinearity issues.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added VIF analysis and discussed multicollinearity. Highly correlated variables were noted but retained as SHAP handles this.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Why were controls not age and sex matched, as these are fixed risk factors for OA? What exclusion criteria were applied to controls? Many EHR codes for OA are common and non-specific — discuss the role of contamination of OA subjects in the control group.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added age and sex matching analysis and discussed potential contamination. Sensitivity analysis was performed excluding borderline cases.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Although they validate their model in a separate sample in UKB, really this needs to be done in a separate cohort. This should be acknowledged.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have acknowledged this limitation in the discussion. The lack of external validation in a non-UKB cohort is noted as a key limitation.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Present the ClinGRS, ClinMet and ClinPro OA risk models using SHAP values similar to how the Clin model was presented in Figure 2D. The sparse volcano plots are not particularly informative.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added SHAP summary plots for all model variants.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: A major missed opportunity: the multi-omics data was not used to disentangle the role of BMI in OA. High BMI is an established predictor but the underlying reasons BMI influences OA etiology are likely diverse. The multi-omics data has potential to identify subgroups of high risk patients.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added a dedicated BMI sub-analysis using multi-omics SHAP values to examine whether different molecular pathways explain the BMI-OA association in different patient subgroups.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors should exercise caution in their claims of causality, as biomarkers may reflect processes already in motion and may not necessarily indicate a causal relationship.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have toned down causal language throughout and explicitly state that associations are observational.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: OA is a heterogeneous condition yet the majority of study participants have an undifferentiated diagnosis. There are considerable differences between joints (e.g., BMI is a bigger risk factor for knee than hip OA). Grouping all OA diagnoses introduces noise.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added joint-specific sub-analyses and acknowledged the heterogeneity limitation in the discussion.

reviewer_strengths.text: Employing interpretable machine learning techniques, the researchers successfully mapped a wide range of OA risk biomarkers. The model's robustness in accurately predicting 70% of OA cases is noteworthy.
The cross-validation approach, well-constructed matched controls, and breadth of variables included are strengths. Very good use of UK Biobank which is almost unique in its size.

entries.paper_title: Artificial intelligence in sepsis early prediction and diagnosis using unstructured data in healthcare
entries.prediction_task: Sepsis early prediction (6-48h before onset)

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The dataset is highly imbalanced; thus, AUC should not be the only performance metric reported. Authors should at least provide PPV and NPV. Furthermore, it is unclear how well calibrated the model is; calibration curves should be provided.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added PPV, NPV, sensitivity, specificity for all time horizons. Calibration curves have been added as supplementary figures.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Based on the title 'role of unstructured data', I would have expected the authors to describe the actual role of clinical notes in prediction performance, in comparison to using structured data only. The results pertain only to processing both types of data together.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added ablation study comparing: structured-only vs. notes-only vs. combined, showing the incremental value of unstructured data.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The method of labelling sepsis prediction is unusual and a potential source of significant confusion: 'when a physician orders for both culture test and lactate test, we classify the patient as one predicted to have sepsis by the physician.' The authors do not provide any evidence to the validity of this crucial statement.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added clinical validation of this labeling approach with references to Rhee et al. 2017 and Singer et al. 2016 Sepsis-3 criteria, and sensitivity analysis with alternative labeling.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: When developing the model, cross-validation is much more robust method to avoid overfitting than the random split used by the authors.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added 5-fold cross-validation results alongside the holdout results, showing consistent performance.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: How was random sampling performed? Was the unit of randomization performed at the level of the note, the patient visit, or the patient? Was there any overlap in patients between the test set and the training/validation set?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Splitting was performed at the patient level. No patient appears in both training and test sets. This has been clarified in the methods.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The paper is missing a demographics table to describe the patient population. What is the incidence of sepsis, severe sepsis, septic shock? How many are admitted to the ICU? Age distribution?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Table 1 has been added with full demographic and clinical characteristics of the cohort.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It would be helpful to include a reliability diagram (calibration diagram) as well as a precision-recall diagram for a representative model to better understand calibration and trade-offs between precision and recall for choosing a decision threshold.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Calibration plots and precision-recall curves have been added as supplementary figures.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: A standard CONSORT enrollment diagram should be included as a figure to show patient flow.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Flow diagram has been added as Figure 1.

reviewer_strengths.text: The background is well motivated. Using ML for real-time surveillance and workflow augmentation for decreasing variability in care is eloquently stated.
Performance characteristics persist even 12 hours prior to sepsis onset (AUC 0.94), which is considerably better than comparison papers.

entries.paper_title: Development of a long noncoding RNA-based machine learning model to predict COVID-19 in-hospital mortality
entries.prediction_task: COVID-19 in-hospital mortality prediction

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The demographics are missing ethnic data which research has shown drastically affect risk assessing algorithms. Key data such as prior medical history, or ongoing treatment for other conditions is important to address or at least mention in limitations.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added demographic and clinical characteristics in Table 1 (diabetes, chronic lung disease, cardiovascular disease, oxygen therapy). Ethnicity was available only in NAPKON cohort. Limitations section updated.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Missing data was imputed without specifying its percentage. For example, was 40% of the age variable missing in cohort A? These characteristics need to be mentioned for assessment of the lncRNA as a potential biomarker.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Missing data percentages have been added to Table 1. In the discovery cohort, 0.5% age, 18.7% smoking were missing. No missing gene expression data.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Was the input data imputed for the validation cohort? If yes, then what were missing proportions? These parameters could skew the results in favor of the biomarker.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Age was the only clinical variable selected for ML from the validation cohort. Since all patients had age information, there was no imputation needed. Results are not skewed.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors do not include reference to the TRIPOD guidelines, which are the gold-standard for reporting risk stratification models.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added TRIPOD checklist compliance as supplementary material.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: AUC says little about performance across the range of risk and interpretation in isolation should be avoided. How do they compare not only in AUC value but in assessing calibration and possible 'real-world' performance through DCA analysis?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added calibration curves and DCA analysis comparing our model with existing COVID-19 mortality prediction models.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: A number of high-quality risk stratification models for predicting inpatient mortality for COVID-19 already exist (see Wynants et al living review in BMJ). What is their comparative performance compared to the novel model described?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added systematic comparison with published COVID-19 mortality models from the Wynants et al. living review.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Another way to further tease apart the relative importance of lncRNA expression would be to show a Shapley beeswarm plot of the feature weights for the models. Ideally we could see this for one of the larger models with additional lncRNAs.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: SHAP beeswarm plots have been added for the expanded model with additional lncRNAs.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It might be possible to improve the model performance using a gradient-boosted tree model. Since this is a very simple code change, it would be worthwhile to see if XGBoost might allow the model to glean additional information from other lncRNAs.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We tested XGBoost and gradient boosting classifiers. Results showed marginal improvement. Added to supplementary comparison table.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: I did not find the file with code.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Code has been uploaded to GitHub and the repository link has been added to the Data Availability section.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: I may have missed something, but I didn't see a link to the code.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Code repository link added.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: I would like to better understand the extent to which LEF1-AS1 expression is independent of age and gender, which are both known risk factors. How correlated is LEF1-AS1 expression with these demographic variables?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: LEF1-AS1 was weakly and negatively correlated to age (r=-0.21 discovery, r=-0.35 validation). Added correlation plot as Figure 2D.

reviewer_strengths.text: The scale of the cohorts is significantly larger than previous work, so the conclusions are more likely to be robust. The classifier performs relatively well, suggesting possible clinical utility.
This is an interesting study with exciting results of translational value.

entries.paper_title: TransformEHR: transformer-based encoder-decoder generative model to enhance prediction of disease outcomes using electronic health records
entries.prediction_task: Disease outcome prediction from longitudinal EHR (pancreatic cancer onset, self-harm in PTSD)

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: AUROC reported only for Pancreatic Cancer in the main manuscript. Supplement tables show Jaccard scores, which is inappropriate for discriminative accuracy. Move main results to main manuscript and report AUROC, AUPRC, and other metrics with best-defined thresholds.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We replaced Jaccard with AUROC as primary metric and added comprehensive metrics to the main manuscript.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: PPV 1.7% - is this really practically useful? If implemented in clinical practice, over 98% of interventions would be for patients who will not actually harm themselves. The statement that PPV 8.45% 'minimizes resource cost' is certainly not true as stated.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have revised the language to more accurately describe the clinical trade-offs. Added cost-effectiveness analysis using ICER thresholds.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Please clarify the meaning of what you are predicting. ICD-10-CM is how the meaning is encoded but does not fully explain what is being predicted. Are these codes entered for billing purposes? Clinical purposes? Without this, it is hard to understand the contribution beyond numerical comparison.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We clarified that ICD-10-CM codes reflect clinical diagnoses documented during VA encounters, and added discussion of billing vs clinical coding practices.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The VA and MIMIC populations are clinically very different (general vs ICU). It is surprising that a system pretrained on a general population performed well on a very different population. More information regarding prediction tasks in different populations needed.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added detailed analysis of domain shift between VA and MIMIC populations and discussed transfer learning properties.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Prediction of pancreatic cancer ICD-10 codes one visit prior may not be clinically useful. The documentation of a code is not equivalent to the first diagnosis. The duration between visits may differ greatly — predicting in 1 year may be much more useful than if next visit is in 1 week.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added a new prediction window (12-36 months) for pancreatic cancer onset and updated results for this clinically meaningful timeframe.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The use of PHI data like actual visit dates will highly impact both usability and generalizability. Recommend using day differences between events instead.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We implemented daysdiff embedding and showed no significant performance difference vs date-specific embedding, while improving privacy protection.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The improvements in PPV over BERT are relatively modest in absolute terms (7.14% vs 8.67%). Is this clinically significant? How much does this practically decrease resource utilization?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added cost-effectiveness analysis showing ICER reduction from baseline, demonstrating practical clinical significance.

reviewer_strengths.text: Methods are well-described and appropriate, with ablation analyses to help determine the most useful model components as well as analyzing model performance in different patient subgroups based on demographics.

entries.paper_title: Biology-guided deep learning predicts prognosis and cancer immunotherapy response
entries.prediction_task: Gastric cancer prognosis and immunotherapy response prediction from CT images

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: A lot more detail needs to be provided on which parts of the CT images were used and correlated to histology images. Which cut of CT was used and why? Were they sagittal or cross-sectional? It is almost impossible to visualize a stomach tumor on CT, especially early stages. It is non-trivial to correlate a biopsy from endoscopy and match to a CT scan.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added detailed description of CT slice selection, tumor segmentation protocol, and histology-radiology correlation methods.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Given that stage is a very good determinant of prognosis, how do we know that the ML model isn't merely measuring tumor size and using this to determine prognosis? What other features other than size is the model using? How do we know it isn't merely using clinicopathological characteristics already readily available?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added ablation analysis removing size-related features and showed the model captures additional information beyond tumor size. Multivariate analysis demonstrates DLS is independent of stage.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: For prediction of benefit for adjuvant chemotherapy, a multivariate analysis should be performed to determine if TME or DLS are independent predictors of benefit from chemotherapy.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added multivariate Cox regression analysis showing DLS is an independent predictor of chemotherapy benefit after adjusting for stage, age, and other clinical variables.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: For immunotherapy treatment — were patients treated with single agent or combination with chemo? If mixed, the analysis needs to be divided to study single agent and combination separately. It is unclear how heterogeneous this group is.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We clarified treatment regimens and performed subgroup analyses by treatment type.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The AUCs seem similar to their previous work (Jiang et al, Lancet Digital Health). Why AUC is used for measuring survival performance? Is the endpoint classification only at 5 years?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We clarified the survival endpoint definition and added time-dependent AUC analysis and C-index for survival prediction.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The choice of being more concerned with interpretability than explainability appears trenchant. If the authors have a strategy for dealing with explainability and determining criteria to select significant features, they should describe it.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We expanded the discussion to address both interpretability (biology-guided architecture) and explainability (feature attribution maps).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: There is a general lack of details (data more than code) for the work to be reproduced.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We expanded methods section with full implementation details and made code available on GitHub.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: How many pathologists were involved in the TME classification? Was this done independently? How were conflicts resolved in TME assessments?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Two pathologists independently classified TME with a third resolving conflicts. Inter-rater agreement (kappa) reported.

reviewer_strengths.text: The results presented are valuable. The methodology is sound. The authors claim superior results compared to the literature.

entries.paper_title: Integration of pathologic characteristics, genetic risk and lifestyle exposure for colorectal cancer survival assessment
entries.prediction_task: Colorectal cancer 5-year survival prediction using polygenic prognostic score + clinical + lifestyle

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: A significant methodological issue: the use of the same dataset for both GWAS and PPS parameterisation. This overlap will result in overfitting of PPS and optimism in performance estimates. This is clearly demonstrated by the drop in performance in the TCGA cohort where calibration and AUC are quite poor compared to the discovery cohorts.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We acknowledge this limitation and have added detailed discussion. We performed sensitivity analysis with stricter separation and noted the performance gap.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Reported statistics are limited to effect sizes (HR), AUC, and KM curves/log rank tests. Reporting of variance explained for the PPS would be helpful, in addition to clinically meaningful metrics such as sensitivity/specificity/PPV, and decision curve analysis.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added variance explained (R²), sensitivity/specificity at optimal thresholds, and DCA analysis.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Overwhelmingly the presence of stage and grade are the strongest predictors of survival (AUC 0.8 vs PRS alone 0.63). Whether the addition of PRS to a model containing stage and grade is of any value needs much more careful consideration than just reporting the increment in AUC.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added NRI analysis and DCA to demonstrate the incremental clinical value of PRS beyond stage/grade.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The combined model has been made publicly available for use 'in clinical practice'. This model has not been externally validated, having been constructed and tested only in the PLCO cohort, and I have very serious reservations about it being made available as such as a clinical tool.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We revised the language to state the tool is for research purposes only, not clinical practice. Added explicit disclaimer.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Handling of missing data noted in Table 1 and several supplementary tables is not reported — was complete case analysis used, or imputation in some form?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We clarified that multiple imputation was used for missing lifestyle variables and complete case analysis for genetic data.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: In the construction of the HLS — it is unclear why these particular predictors were chosen and how cut-off thresholds were defined. The 'traditional model' includes some but not all lifestyle predictors. Authors reference a pre-existing validated lifestyle model (Cheng et al) — is there a reason this was not used?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We justified predictor selection based on WHO guidelines and existing literature. Comparison with Cheng et al model added.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The paper does not report how cancer cases were identified in UKB (which field was used). End of follow-up/censoring dates should also be defined, as cancer data has been regularly updated.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added case identification methodology (ICD-10 codes from cancer registry) and specified censoring dates.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: I would suggest that the number of cases does not constitute 'Large scale' GWAS meta-analysis. There is insufficient power to detect GWAS-significant SNP associations. This should be made clearer in the discussion.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We toned down the 'large scale' claim and added power analysis discussion.

reviewer_strengths.text: An interesting and innovative study that firstly introduces PPS (a germline variant score) into the colorectal cancer survival prediction. Multi-ancestry replication is a strength.

entries.paper_title: Development and validation of an interpretable model integrating multimodal information for improving ovarian cancer diagnosis
entries.prediction_task: Ovarian cancer diagnosis from ultrasound + clinical variables

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Identifying ovarian cancer in a woman with CA125 of 10,000 or massive ascites is not difficult. What would be of actual clinical value is an algorithm that is highly predictive in women with NORMAL CA125s, relatively small masses (<10 cm), without obvious clinical evidence of malignancy.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We showed that 44.6% had normal CA125 and 82.6% had lesions <10cm. OvcaFinder still achieved highest performance in these subgroups.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Nearly half of the training set of 724 masses were malignant, likely introducing significant bias limiting generalizability. In community settings, typically <5% of masses are malignant. Even in tertiary referral centers, usual prevalence is <25%.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We acknowledged the relatively higher malignancy rate in the limitation section. Both centers were high-level cancer hospitals in China. Added discussion of prevalence adjustment.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Inclusion of borderline tumors as malignant is problematic. Borderline tumors rarely cause death and surgery by gynecologic oncologist has no impact on survival. Show performance if only invasive cancers are included.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added sensitivity analysis excluding borderline tumors showing maintained performance for invasive cancers.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: In assessing ORADS, sensitivity dropped from 96.2% (internal) to 85.7% (external). A difference between 96% and 86% is significant. An explanation as to why performance varied so much between external and internal datasets is needed.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We analyzed sources of performance degradation and attributed differences to imaging equipment, operator expertise, and patient population differences between centers.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The unusual nature of the training set (nearly 50% malignant) and the lack of detail about how human input was provided makes it impossible to reproduce the work.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We expanded methods with full HITL protocol details, reader selection criteria, and scoring methodology.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors did not explain what DL specifically finds in ultrasound images. The explanation that it 'highlighted the most important areas' is laconic. Should explain what extent and localization of hotspots mean in benign vs malignant lesions.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added quantitative analysis of Grad-CAM hotspot patterns comparing benign vs malignant, including hotspot area percentage and spatial distribution.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Development of RF model serving as OvcaFinder lacks details. How were the sets of different predictors identified? Please expand the description.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We expanded the RF model development section with feature selection process and hyperparameter tuning details.

reviewer_strengths.text: The work is interesting in that there is significant interest in ML models for diagnostic imaging. No previously reported ML model used a similar strategy, so the report is novel.

entries.paper_title: Targeted plasma proteomics reveals organ damage signatures of AIDS- and noncommunicable disease-related deaths in people with HIV
entries.prediction_task: Mortality prediction in HIV patients using plasma proteomics panel

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Selection bias may be a concern as less than 6% of the original CHART cohort is included. How do baseline characteristics of selected patients compare to the overall population? Could patients have been matched with ART treatment in addition to age and sex?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added comparison of selected vs overall cohort characteristics and justified the sampling strategy. ART matching was not feasible due to heterogeneity.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Adjustments for the duration or type of ART use are conspicuously missing from the models. Several ART either act directly on viral or host proteins or indirectly through transcription. This could enhance models' accuracy.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added ART duration and type as covariates in sensitivity analyses. Results remained robust after adjustment.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Adjusting protein expression for renal function is important as several studies report the impact of renal function on protein expression due to the kidney's role in filtering and inflammatory response.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added eGFR as a covariate and performed sensitivity analysis stratified by renal function.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Throughout the study, the authors implied seeking unique proteomics signatures dichotomizing AIDS vs NCD deaths. However, figures compare each death type with HIV survivors separately. The conclusions could be totally different if all groups were compared against each other. A Venn diagram showing common proteins across all comparisons is needed.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added comprehensive multi-group comparison analysis with Venn diagram and pairwise contrasts.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The paper fails to describe potential confounders. The time of plasma isolation and preservative type could introduce methodological artifacts. The time between plasma collection and death is not described. Authors state protein expression was altered 'right before' death but provide no time data.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We clarified sample collection protocols, added time-to-death analysis, and corrected temporal language.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The statistical approaches were not clear. Table 1 showed three P-values where ANOVA followed by post-hoc test should have been used. Tables include data not significant after FDR correction, making interpretation difficult.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We corrected statistical tests and removed non-significant results from main tables.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It is not clear why the validation cohort of 127 samples had significantly lower sensitivity than the training datasets. Supplemental Table 1 is missing.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We explained the performance gap due to smaller sample size and different clinical characteristics. Supplemental Table 1 added.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Several unsubstantiated statements imply causality throughout the results section. Introduction states 'traditional biomarkers are challenging for predicting mortality' but Discussion says they have 'potential for predicting mortality' — these are contradictory.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We revised causal language to associational framing and resolved the logical inconsistency between introduction and discussion.

reviewer_strengths.text: The report is appropriately written with appropriate statistical methods, prediction corrections, and a validation group. The markers identified (CA12, CA14) are consistent and potentially biologically relevant.

entries.paper_title: Real-time prediction of intensive care unit patient acuity and therapy requirements using state-space modelling
entries.prediction_task: ICU patient acuity and life-sustaining therapy prediction (4-hour horizon)

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The motivation for using Mamba is not clear. There doesn't seem to be a significant difference between APRICOT-T (Transformer) and APRICOT-M (Mamba). CatBoost and GRU appear competitive on many tasks while requiring far less computational resources.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added computational cost comparison and showed Mamba advantages in longer sequences and inference speed.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Confidence intervals computed using bootstrapping provide uncertainty related to the data sample but not related to model parameters. Also, using time-to-event analysis rather than binary classification could avoid issues related to time window choice.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We acknowledged this limitation and discussed model uncertainty vs data uncertainty. Time-to-event analysis added as supplementary comparison.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The abstract states the model 'was validated prospectively on data from 2021-2023' but Mamba was first introduced in 2023. It appears the model was 'retrospectively validated' on previously collected prospective data. Please clarify.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We clarified that the prospective data collection preceded model development, and the model was applied retrospectively to this prospectively collected dataset.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: One challenge with prediction of rare events is having low PPV. AUC tends to produce overly optimistic results. It would be insightful to repeat analysis in 50 patients from prospective cohort by at least three clinical adjudicators to determine clinical utility (were alerts timely, accurate, actionable?).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added clinician review of alerts in a subset of prospective patients with assessment of timeliness and actionability.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Authors claim 'first SSM model application to clinical data' but there are multiple prior studies applying state-space models to clinical data (Yin 2021, Ghassemi 2017, Nemati 2013). Please explain how the proposed SSM differs from prior works.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We corrected the novelty claim to 'first Mamba-based SSM application' and added comparison with prior SSM clinical works.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Results for the temporal cohort were relegated to supplementary material. An extra column for the temporal cohort would not take up much space in the main article.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We moved temporal validation results to the main text.

reviewer_strengths.text: Major strength is that the model was validated on external, temporally shifted and prospectively collected data. Performed significantly better than the traditional SOFA score.
The curation and harmonization of such diverse datasets require tremendous efforts, and the authors should be applauded for their dedication.

entries.paper_title: Predicting in-hospital outcomes of patients with acute kidney injury
entries.prediction_task: In-hospital mortality and dialysis prediction in AKI patients (24h-7d)

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The use of a bidirectional RNN at any given point in time is using future data which would not be available for clinical decision. That is the point of a bidirectional RNN and the point of this criticism. Evaluation would be overly optimistic. This is a major flaw in the paper.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We clarified that the bidirectional component operates within the historical data window only, not across the prediction boundary. Added unidirectional LSTM comparison.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The use of data from 20 past years is problematic — medicine has taken a great leap forward. Using a temporally remote population to predict future patients may not work. Instead of randomly splitting, temporal partitioning would more accurately estimate deployment performance.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added temporal split analysis using recent years for testing and discussed limitations of using historical data.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: AUROCs on the derivation set of 95% are expected. I cannot imagine why they report these results and claim good performance. I want to know the results on the test set properly designed as a reliable estimate of future performance.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We reorganized results to lead with test set performance and de-emphasized training metrics.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: They do not present precision-recall curves which some might consider better measures with severe class imbalance. Death rate is only 1.3% leaving marked class imbalance.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added precision-recall curves and AUPRC for all prediction tasks.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It is not clear how features were actually merged from 24-hour epochs. How were values combined — average, range, median, mean? It would not be possible to reproduce these models and test the results or apply them clinically.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added detailed feature engineering description with aggregation functions (mean, min, max, last) for each variable type.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: On numerous occasions they say that identifying patients at risk will improve their outcome — that is a hope rather than a proven reality; they should avoid the hyperbole.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We toned down claims about clinical outcome improvement and framed as potential benefit requiring prospective validation.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Results appearing in the discussion and methods appearing throughout. Comparators only show up in discussion where they don't belong. Paper presented in a somewhat jumbled fashion.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We reorganized the manuscript to separate methods, results, and discussion clearly.

reviewer_strengths.text: Respectable ML attempt using large amounts of retrospective data from three different hospitals, enhancing generalizability.

entries.paper_title: Enhancing the diagnosis of functionally relevant coronary artery disease with machine learning
entries.prediction_task: Functionally relevant CAD prediction from stress ECG + clinical variables

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: AUROC of 0.71 for best-performing model is modest. The NPV of 0.89 at 15% threshold will be challenging for clinical practice, especially when the approach aims to reduce unnecessary testing. Authors should more clearly justify optimal thresholds.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added clinical impact analysis showing that even modest AUROC translates to meaningful reduction (15-17%) in unnecessary imaging referrals.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Major concern: the primary outcome 'functionally relevant CAD' is a combination of two outcomes (myocardial ischemia by SPECT + obstructive CAD on cath) without clear delineation. Selective referral to angiography induces bias since clinical aspects used by the ML model also influence decisions to pursue angiography.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We separated analyses by outcome type and added discussion of verification bias from selective referral patterns.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: ECG features in SHAP analysis are not adequately addressed. Are there aspects that identify ECG components of interest? Are there at least positive and negative examples that are meaningful? Summary statistics across positive and negative studies would make assessment more objective.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We expanded SHAP analysis with ECG-specific feature interpretation, positive/negative examples, and aggregate statistics.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The data sources in both internal and external validation require more details. What were the clinical settings? Were patients consecutive? Why were patients dropped for 1 missing observation? How many were dropped?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added detailed data source descriptions, patient flow diagrams, and missing data handling documentation.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The collaborative model, touted as most successful, is unclear. How is post-test judgment quantified? How is it combined numerically?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added detailed description of the logistic regression combining ML scores and cardiologist post-test probability.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: In Fig. 2, Sensitivity and Precision were shown. It is good idea to present Specificity, Recall, Accuracy and F1 score as well.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added complete metric panel including specificity, recall, accuracy, and F1.

reviewer_strengths.text: The paper provides a good framework of how to complement cardiologist by using this ML framework. The dataset (3522 patients) with cardiologist validation is an important feature.
Comprehensive study including model development and external testing. The most novel aspect is automatic incorporation of stress ECG data.

entries.paper_title: Stratification of hospitalised COVID-19 patients into clinical severity progression groups by immuno-phenotyping and machine learning
entries.prediction_task: COVID-19 clinical severity progression prediction from immunophenotyping

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: There seems to be arbitrary reasoning for defining different immunophenotypes. Based on antibody/cytokine profile, first 3 patients in EXI group should be classified as LAI. This becomes even more subjective for the Barcelona validation cohort. Individuals should be accurately grouped and data reanalyzed.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We provided detailed cluster assignment justification with sensitivity analysis showing robustness to boundary cases.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Healthy individuals are not the appropriate controls for COVID-19. Please include age-matched hospitalized patients with phenotypically similar disease states to identify differences unique to SARS-CoV-2 infection.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We acknowledged this limitation and discussed the difficulty of obtaining appropriate disease-matched controls during the pandemic.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Significant difference in gender between the 3 immunophenotypes — more males in EXI and LAI. Whole data could be explained by higher propensity of males for proinflammatory cytokines. Statistical analysis should be reanalyzed normalizing for age, gender, and DFSO using multivariate analysis.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added multivariate analysis adjusting for age, gender, and DFSO. Immunophenotype effects remained significant after adjustment.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Lot of overlap in the data and significance is driven by few outliers especially in EXI group. May be just driven by these few outliers in EXI/LAI compared with BRI.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We performed robust analysis excluding outliers and showed consistent findings.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: IL-6, IL-8 and IL-10 are main markers of disease severity and their levels can easily explain disease outcome among immunotypes. So that brings into question the rationale of the whole study.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We showed that immunophenotyping provides additional prognostic value beyond these individual cytokines through interaction effects.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Authors conclude this immunophenotyping can be applied rapidly in clinic. It's unclear how this extensive analysis can be practically applied where the patient deteriorates in days — during pandemic with shortage of resources, this approach is impractical.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We toned down clinical implementation claims and discussed this as a research framework rather than a point-of-care tool.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The sample sizes are relatively small (primary cohort ~100 patients). Authors have used sensitivity analysis for accuracy vs test size which is good, but inherent limitations remain.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We acknowledged sample size limitation and showed consistent results in the validation cohort.

reviewer_strengths.text: This is a solid manuscript. A great example of how machine learning can be used to provide insights into phenotypes of diseases. Thorough and robust sensitivity analysis for accuracy vs test size increases confidence.

entries.paper_title: At-home wearables and machine learning sensitively capture disease progression in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
entries.prediction_task: ALS disease progression tracking and severity prediction from wearable accelerometers

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors focus on rate of change, but variability in rates between patients plays a significant role. These two factors determine 'sensitivity' of a longitudinal marker (signal to noise). Could the authors provide insight into variability between patients relative to the average rate of decline?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added between-patient variability analysis showing coefficient of variation for each feature's rate of change.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The monitoring protocol is quite extensive with 4 accelerometers per patient. Could the authors provide insight into adherence? How many patients managed to complete the 7-day wear-time period? Metrics of patient burden and retention would be insightful.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added adherence statistics showing completion rates, dropout reasons, and wear-time compliance by visit.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: From the methods it is unclear how the rate of decline was calculated. There are no longitudinal models reported. It looks like per-patient regression was fitted and slope extracted, but this information is not provided — the statistical analysis cannot be replicated.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added detailed description of per-patient linear mixed-effects models used to estimate rates of decline.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The ICC is based on 'first half vs second half of days'. This likely gives a systematic difference as patients may be more active in the first half due to fatigue. Day 1 vs Day 2 comparison would be more accurate.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added day-by-day ICC analysis as supplementary comparison.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Using 'the limb with the fastest progression rate' has complexities. This can be done after data collection, but for clinical trials outcomes must be prespecified — this could result in increased type 1 error.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We discussed this limitation for clinical trial application and suggested prespecifying the primary limb based on initial assessment.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The pairwise comparison model description is lacking clarity. The formula and outcome encoding need clearer explanation for the less statistical reader.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We rewrote the pairwise model description with step-by-step worked example.

reviewer_strengths.text: The 'pairwise model' approach, disregarding the clinical outcome and using only longitudinal wearable data, is a major strength — an imperfect prediction of the ALSFRS-R is actually desired as one wants to improve on what it measures.
Phenomenal study and manuscript. Study protocol is robust and well-executed, data analysis is novel for the clinical field. This will be extremely valuable to the field going forward.

entries.paper_title: Shareable artificial intelligence to extract cancer outcomes from electronic health records for precision oncology research
entries.prediction_task: Cancer outcome extraction from imaging reports and oncologist notes (teacher-student privacy-preserving)

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: There is no evidence that there actually is any data leakage in the classification model in the first place — therefore it is not clear there is anything to be fixed, which is the objective of the paper. Classification models learn category assignments, not patient-specific information.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added discussion clarifying the precautionary principle and referenced recent membership inference attacks on clinical NLP models.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The proposed models are not compared with any other methods, only an uninformative model. LLMs like ChatGPT have been proven effective for extracting structured data from clinical notes. Open-source LLMs on in-house servers could protect privacy without the teacher-student paradigm.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added comparison with GPT-4 and open-source LLM baselines, showing trade-offs between accuracy, cost, and privacy.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: What is the benefit of training the student model with soft logit output vs hard prediction labels? There is only a difference between soft and hard labels. Authors need to illustrate benefits of soft label training.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added ablation comparing soft vs hard label training showing soft labels preserve calibration and improve minority class performance.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It should be stressed that the privacy-preserving approach has only been demonstrated to work on the relatively narrowly defined task of outcome extraction. A richer illustration in Figure 1 showing data boundaries would help.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added clearer figure showing data flow boundaries and scoped the claims to outcome extraction tasks.

reviewer_strengths.text: The analyses credibly demonstrate the feasibility of a privacy-preserving teacher-student paradigm for outcome detection on imaging and oncology reports.

entries.paper_title: Synthesize high-dimensional longitudinal electronic health records via hierarchical autoregressive language model
entries.prediction_task: Synthetic EHR generation for downstream disease prediction tasks

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Show standard deviations (confidence intervals) in Tables 7 and 8. Performance improvement seems mainly from the transformer backbone, limiting the specific contributions of the proposed method.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added CIs and provided ablation analysis showing contributions of each component beyond the transformer backbone.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: My fundamental objection to nearly all synthetic data papers: Is the real input data available? Is the synthetic data available? Where is the public code repository? They cannot answer 'yes' to all three. How could someone reproduce this?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We released code on GitHub, made synthetic MIMIC data available, and documented that the claims data is proprietary but synthetic output is shareable.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Which modules or components are specifically devised for handling the high-dimension issue? This should be more clearly discussed.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added focused discussion of the masked linear layer for high-dimensional intra-visit modeling and transformer for inter-visit modeling.

reviewer_strengths.text: Noteworthy and significant — simultaneously addresses high-dimensionality, longitudinal coherency, and continuous variables. Evaluation of data quality checking and privacy analysis is thorough.

entries.paper_title: Radiogenomic signatures reveal multiscale intratumour heterogeneity associated with biological functions and survival in breast cancer
entries.prediction_task: Breast cancer survival prediction from MRI radiomics + genomic features

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The model has too many parameters. 24 parameters with 47+40 cases — model is overparametrized. Maximum ~8-10 parameters. They've got (10+10+19)×3=117 parameters — almost infinite ways to extract n from 117 to build models. How did they arrive at these models/parameters?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We performed LASSO regularization with nested cross-validation and reported the number of retained features. Added comparison with simpler models.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Calculated subtraction images without dividing by precontrast image — makes comparison of histogram features (mean, range, min, max) across patients highly dubious. Both in-plane resolution and slice thickness vary — should interpolate to same resolution prior to feature calculations.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added image normalization and resampling to uniform resolution. Results remain consistent after standardization.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: None of the prognosis analyses correct for common clinical features such as age, size, grade, stage, hormone receptor status. It is important to know if the radiogenomic biomarkers are independent of these clinical features.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added multivariate Cox regression adjusting for age, stage, grade, and receptor status. Radiogenomic signature remained an independent predictor.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Figure 4d and 7d appear to be training set performance — if so should NOT be reported as it is not representative of unseen data.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We clarified these are cross-validated results, not training performance, and relabeled figures.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Several gene expression signatures for breast cancer (Mammaprint, OncotypeDX) are clinically used. Authors have to study how their proposed biomarkers add additional prognostic value on top of these existing prognostic biomarkers.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added comparison with established genomic signatures and showed complementary prognostic information.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: IRB/informed consent information not provided. Radiomics methodology needs more detail — software validation, grey level reduction, normalization method.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added IRB information and detailed radiomics methodology including software (PyRadiomics), grey levels, and normalization steps.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: MRI data quality is no longer state-of-the-art/outdated. Since the TCGA/I-SPY studies there have been significant improvements in MRI software and hardware. Results may not be representative of current MRI radiomics potential.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We acknowledged the data age limitation and discussed how modern MRI would likely improve results.

reviewer_strengths.text: Solid paper with good design using multiple publicly available datasets. The idea has never been performed in breast cancer and results are very promising. Very well written and logical.

entries.paper_title: An ensemble penalized regression method for multi-ancestry polygenic risk prediction
entries.prediction_task: Multi-ancestry polygenic risk prediction (PROSPER method)

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Given the very good performance of 'weighted lassosum2', I wonder whether the extra gain from PROSPER comes from the L2-penalty sharing effects across populations, or from the super learning step? You could also add super learning step for lassosum2 to answer this question.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added ablation: super learning alone on lassosum2 vs PROSPER's L2 penalty. Both contribute, but L2 penalty provides the larger gain.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Is it reasonable to assume genetic effects are similarly similar across populations (constant c)? I might expect this similarity to decrease with genetic distance between populations. Any literature to support either claim?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We cited literature supporting similar effect sizes across closely related populations and acknowledged this may break down for more distant populations.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: LD references computed from 1000G. Have you tried using more individuals (e.g., UKBB)? AMR in 1000G is used for Latino ancestry — is it really the same ancestry?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We compared 1000G vs UKBB LD references showing minimal impact for European ancestry but noted limitations for admixed populations.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Analysis code is publicly shared but I cannot find the code corresponding to LDpred2 analyses. I am surprised LDpred2 performs consistently worse than lassosum2 — maybe consider extending the grid to the one currently recommended in the tutorial.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added LDpred2 code and re-ran with recommended grid parameters. Performance gap narrowed but PROSPER still outperforms.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Did the authors consider using machine learning methods for the super-learner step? Also, how large a tuning dataset would you recommend?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We tested ML methods (random forest, gradient boosting) in the super-learner — linear combination performed comparably. Added tuning set size sensitivity analysis.

reviewer_strengths.text: The method is clearly presented with comprehensive comparisons with existing methods and applied to various real datasets.

entries.paper_title: Tuning parameters for polygenic risk score methods using GWAS summary statistics from training data
entries.prediction_task: PRS parameter tuning without external validation data (PRStuning method)

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: For PRStuning based on C+T, AUC increases when threshold decreases. For LDpred, highest AUC is at parameter 0.3. Is this an indication of overfitting or convergence issues? Based on Tables 4 and 5, is it concluded that P+T is better than LDpred?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We clarified that this pattern reflects the polygenicity of the trait. Added convergence diagnostics for LDpred Gibbs chains.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Would it be possible to include confounders such as age, sex as part of the AUC calculation?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We showed that covariate adjustment has minimal impact on relative ranking of PRS methods but added adjusted AUC as supplementary analysis.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: How does the method handle the HLA region of Chromosome 6? Is the chosen LD radius (5) large enough? Please define LD radius in terms of SNPs/megabase pairs.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We defined LD radius as 5Mb and showed that the HLA region is adequately captured. Added sensitivity analysis with larger radius.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: As summary statistics of T2D, CAD, and IBD are available, could authors generate PRS using traditional LDpred2 with UKBB data and compare AUC with LDpred based PRStuning? Include computational time comparison.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added traditional LDpred2 comparison and computational time benchmarks showing PRStuning is 10× faster.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Author mentioned they applied the framework in European ancestral group only. Would it be possible to include non-European population in the training datasets?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We acknowledged European-only limitation and discussed extension to multi-ancestry as future work.

reviewer_strengths.text: Novel approach offering two significant advantages: eliminates need for external validation data and is computationally efficient. The Empirical Bayes approach is well-motivated.

entries.paper_title: Utility of polygenic scores across diverse diseases in a hospital cohort for predictive modeling
entries.prediction_task: Cross-ancestry PRS evaluation across 457 phenotypes in Taiwanese hospital cohort

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Several factors affect PRS prediction quality — sample sizes of source data, genetic architecture, and model used — but authors did not assess correlation of source GWAS sample sizes with prediction quality. Did not establish overlap with their genotyping data. Did not explore why ankylosing spondylitis had highest prediction while heart failure had lowest.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added correlation analysis between source GWAS sample size, SNP overlap, heritability, and prediction quality across all 457 traits.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: In the abstract, authors stated significant incremental predictive performance, but the methods and results do not include any analyses investigating the incremental performance of PGS — only full model analyses with covariates were included.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added incremental analysis: PGS-only model vs covariates-only vs combined, with delta-AUC and NRI for each trait.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Were PGS from all ancestry used, or only PGS trained from East Asian samples? Was there any attempt at handling population stratification? Were there any attempts to avoid sample overlap?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We included all-ancestry PGS and added population stratification adjustment via principal components. Assessed and excluded overlapping samples.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: For the t-test and Wilcoxon test, were there any attempts to control for covariates such as age, sex, and population stratification? Was the metric reported based on PGS only, or the full model?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We clarified that all association tests control for age, sex, and top 10 PCs. Both PGS-only and full model metrics now reported.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Figure 1 annotations unclear — n and m were not annotated. Add a box between 'Access medical records' and 'Identified phenotype' stating post-QC sample size.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We improved Figure 1 with clear annotations for sample sizes at each step.

reviewer_strengths.text: A great resource that will inform researchers working in East Asian ancestry populations on trait-specific transferability of cross-ancestry disease predictions.

entries.paper_title: Explainable multimodal deep learning for predicting thyroid cancer lateral lymph node metastasis using ultrasound imaging
entries.prediction_task: Thyroid cancer lateral lymph node metastasis prediction from multimodal data

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Lacks thorough comparison with existing baselines. Comprehensive ablation studies needed for each component and each modality's independent contribution.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added baseline comparisons and comprehensive ablation.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Predicting microscopic LLNMs with AI may be HARMFUL — removal of small metastases may not change outcome. Will result in overutilization of lateral neck dissection.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added LLNM characteristics analysis stratified by clinical significance. Revised workflow.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: DCA assumes all true AI predictions are beneficial — not true for microscopic metastases. Proposed workflow would not be best clinical management.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Revised DCA accounting for clinically insignificant metastases.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Comparison with human experts unfair due to differing dataset sizes (model on full data vs radiologists on N=200).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added model performance on same N=200 subset.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: LLNM-Net trained on cancerous nodules only — most thyroid nodules are benign. Cannot be used for population screening.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Clarified intended use is pre-surgical planning, not screening.

reviewer_strengths.text: Performance impressive, quality of data science is high. Using AI to identify thyroid locations associated with metastatic disease is useful.

entries.paper_title: Medical multimodal multitask foundation model for lung cancer screening
entries.prediction_task: Lung cancer screening: nodule detection, risk prediction, CVD mortality from LDCT + clinical text

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: CVD mortality as binary label is over-simplification — it is right-censored time-to-event data. Should stratify by cut-off years like cancer risk task.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added time-stratified CVD analysis.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Clinical metadata encoded as predefined-rule text — fundamentally differs from natural language. Is this necessary vs simply encoding as array?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added ablation comparing text vs tabular encoding.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: AUC improvements for MT-MM are small in some cases. Need critical perspective balancing gains vs extra effort.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added cost analysis and honest discussion of marginal gains.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Heatmaps show apparently useless tokens ('brother', '142') as important. Can multi-source information be shown to be composed in complementary way?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added token-level attribution analysis.

reviewer_strengths.text: First multimodal multitask pretrained FM for LDCT screening. Superior performance over SOTA.

entries.paper_title: Multimodal histopathologic models stratify hormone receptor-positive early breast cancer
entries.prediction_task: Breast cancer recurrence risk from histopathology (Orpheus vs Oncotype DX)

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Correlation of 0.6 does not indicate reliable individual prediction. No individual-level performance data vs gold-standard. Need calibration plot with censoring.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added individual-level analysis and calibration plots.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Cut-off in Orpheus for high-risk classification not specified. Does it vary across populations?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Reported cut-off with cross-cohort sensitivity analysis.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Claim that Orpheus enhances beyond Oncotype DX needs tempering — linear models developed within Oncotype risk groups, comparison may not be equitable.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Tempered claims and added independent evaluation.

reviewer_strengths.text: Interdisciplinary expertise in biostatistics, computational oncology, statistical learning, and computer science.

entries.paper_title: Quantifying portable genetic effects and improving cross-ancestry genetic prediction with GWAS summary statistics
entries.prediction_task: Cross-ancestry polygenic risk prediction (X-Wing method)

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Type I error simulations only 100 times — not enough at 0.05 level. Need ≥1,000. Also need FDR threshold sensitivity analysis.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Increased to 1,000 simulations with FDR sensitivity.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Only simulated on chromosome 22 — heritability disproportionally large, samples highly related. Need whole-genome simulation.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added whole-genome simulations.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Only East Asian and European. Transferability to African samples is harder. Should apply to AFR samples.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added African ancestry analysis using PAGE.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: X-Wing only marginally better than PRS-CSx. Need scenario simulations showing when each method wins.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added scenario-based simulations.

reviewer_strengths.text: Addresses important issue of cross-ancestry PRS using summary-level data only. Clearly written.

entries.paper_title: Development and external validation of prediction algorithms to improve early diagnosis of cancer
entries.prediction_task: Early cancer diagnosis prediction for 15 cancer types from primary care EHR

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Time horizon for prediction not found — paramount importance. Are models predicting imminent diagnoses or long-term risk? Models with very high AUC may just be diagnosing established cancers.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Clarified 2-year window and added time-stratified analyses.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Fundamental difference between predicting probability cancer is already present vs probability of developing cancer in the future. These concepts are conflated.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Revised terminology: 'risk of cancer diagnosis' instead of 'cancer risk'.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Missing data shown not to be MCAR. Imputation method doesn't handle MNAR. Need reporting of N missing and bias analysis.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added MNAR sensitivity analysis.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Variables kept based on P values. Did you consider data-driven variable selection?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added LASSO comparison showing similar results.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Calibration intercept/slope should be in main text. Blood tests add almost nothing — discuss clinical implications.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added calibration to main text, discussed limited value of blood tests.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: DCA not commonly used — need explanation. Cancer-specific DCA needed, aggregate 'any cancer' DCA makes little sense.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added cancer-specific DCA with interpretation.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Model coefficients and variables need to be clearly provided to allow further validation.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Provided full coefficients in supplementary tables.

reviewer_strengths.text: Well-written. Multi-variable models for 15 cancer types using large-scale primary care data.

entries.paper_title: A noninvasive model for chronic kidney disease screening and common pathological type identification from retinal images
entries.prediction_task: CKD screening, pathological diagnosis and prognosis from retinal fundus images

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Sample size lacks formal power calculations and has concerning issues in key subgroups like Somalia cohort (n=47) and less common pathological types like MCD/FSGS. This raises questions about statistical power.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added power calculations and explicitly stated limited power for rare subtypes. Somalia cohort results reported with appropriate caveats.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Missing data handling lacks adequate documentation — no clear explanation of how missing values were managed, no reporting of missing data percentages, no sensitivity analyses to assess impact.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added missing data reporting, imputation methodology, and sensitivity analysis.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Model calibration is insufficiently reported — calibration plots relegated to supplementary materials, no formal calibration testing (such as Hosmer-Lemeshow) presented.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We moved calibration plots to main figures and added Hosmer-Lemeshow test results.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Multiple testing concerns remain unaddressed — no clear adjustment for multiple comparisons across numerous statistical tests performed.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons and flagged results that do not survive correction.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors categorize MCD or FSGS as combined feature. It is reasonable to combine primary MCD/FSGS as podocytopathies, but secondary FSGS is much more frequent and has different clinical management.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We discussed the MCD/FSGS distinction and added sensitivity analysis separating primary vs secondary FSGS.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The Net Reclassification Index (NRI) has well-documented issues with the category-free version and should be interpreted with caution. The term 'metadata' is confusing — it relates to actual clinical data, not metadata.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We clarified NRI limitations and changed 'metadata' to 'clinical data' throughout.

reviewer_strengths.text: Authors are very clear in methodology and present compelling results using high-quality data including multi-national datasets. Excellent visuals and clear clinical implications.
Prediction of disease progression and pathological diagnosis, comparison with human performance, and validation in prospective and external cohorts is relevant. Methodology is sound.

entries.paper_title: Prehospital real-time AI for trauma mortality prediction: a multi-institutional and multi-national validation study
entries.prediction_task: Emergency room mortality prediction in trauma patients from prehospital data

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The model was developed and internally validated in South Korean trauma centers. External validation in Australia (n=3,578) is valuable but limited to one center. Performance in other healthcare systems (e.g., US, European EMS) would strengthen generalizability claims.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We acknowledged geographic limitation and discussed plans for broader international validation. Added sensitivity analysis by injury mechanism.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Calibration analysis should be presented more prominently. The model's predicted probabilities vs observed mortality rates should be clearly shown across risk groups.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We moved calibration plots to main figures and added calibration metrics (slope, intercept, Brier score).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: How would this model be deployed in real-time prehospital settings? What are the latency requirements? What happens when data is missing (common in trauma settings)?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We described the real-time deployment architecture, measured inference latency (<1s), and added analysis of model robustness to missing prehospital variables.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The study follows TRIPOD+AI and TRIPOD-cluster guidelines — this is commendable. Minor formatting improvements needed in checklist compliance table.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We reformatted the TRIPOD+AI checklist table.

reviewer_strengths.text: Large-scale study with 204,189 patients for development and multi-national external validation. Follows TRIPOD+AI guidelines rigorously.
Clinically important application — prehospital mortality prediction could meaningfully improve triage decisions and resource allocation.

entries.paper_title: Machine learning models identify predictive features of patient mortality across dementia types
entries.prediction_task: Mortality prediction across dementia types (1-10 year thresholds)

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Authors should provide rationale why selecting XGBoost, not other ML models. Unclear whether further feature selection can improve performance.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added comparison with RF, LR, SVM. XGBoost selected for best AUC and interpretability via TreeSHAP.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Class imbalance is a major issue — subjects at later stages naturally have higher mortality. Difference between 1-year and 10-year models may simply reflect class imbalance rather than genuine finding. Need class-balanced resampling or class-weighted loss.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added class-weighted analysis and SMOTE sensitivity analysis. Results robust to rebalancing.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Missing result figures. Discussion mentions survival analysis differed across dementia types but corresponding figures cannot be found in manuscript or supplementary material.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added missing survival curves by dementia subtype.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Model performance evaluated only with AUC. Additional metrics like sensitivity, specificity, F1, and calibration should be reported for clinical applicability.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added full metric panel including sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, F1.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Whether adding genetic or multi-omics data may improve prediction further in future studies should be discussed.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added discussion of potential for genomic/proteomic data integration.

reviewer_strengths.text: Important and novel ML study for dementia precision medicine. Potential application for future clinical studies and patient care.
Survival analysis stratified by comorbidities is a strength. Use of SHAP for feature importance evaluation is a strength.

entries.paper_title: An interpretable machine learning algorithm enables dynamic 48-hour mortality prediction during an ICU stay
entries.prediction_task: Dynamic 48-hour ICU mortality prediction with 24h update cycle

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The study lacks external validation. Model should be tested in very different conditions to avoid out-of-distribution bias.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Acknowledged as limitation and discussed plans for multi-center validation.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Why LightGBM as first choice? There are many time-series models like LSTM that may better capture temporal patterns. Also, SOFA score uses much less variables — for parsimony, SOFA seems better for practical use.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Compared with LSTM and showed LightGBM competitive. SOFA comparison added showing ML model significantly outperforms.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The outcome variable is imbalanced data. What is the proportion of deceased during the time frame?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added mortality proportion and class imbalance handling discussion.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Will stacked ensemble model further improve performance? There is evidence that ensemble models achieve better accuracy than any individual model alone.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Discussed ensemble potential in future directions.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Why update every 24 hours to predict 48-hour mortality, rather than every hour or every 6/12 hours for shorter horizons? Need clear rationale for this design choice.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added clinical rationale: 24h update aligns with ICU rounding schedules and clinical decision cycles.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: PPV remains low indicating many false alarms. How to interpret or handle these false alarms?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added false alarm analysis with risk stratification tiers to reduce alarm fatigue.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: While model accuracy is important, it may not translate to clinical benefits such as reducing mortality in ICU. More work needed to test effectiveness.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added discussion of implementation pathway and need for prospective impact study.

reviewer_strengths.text: The effort to stratify patient risk is commendable, as prediction is not the ultimate goal. Threshold selection analysis is interesting.

entries.paper_title: Machine learning for early dynamic prediction of functional outcome after stroke
entries.prediction_task: 3-month mortality and functional status prediction after ischemic stroke from first 72h data

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Most literature uses discharge data for 3-month outcomes, or uses time-varying data for in-hospital outcomes. Using 72h data to predict 3-month outcome — by the time prediction is made, patient status will change many times. Median LOS is 7-10 days for ischemic stroke. The 72h prediction becomes irrelevant. Authors should either predict at discharge, or predict in-hospital outcomes.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added analysis at discharge timepoint and discussed clinical decision points where 72h prediction is relevant (early transfer decisions).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Significant risk of cherry-picking models when there is no bootstrapping with multiple random splits. While authors bootstrap the CV procedure, they need equivalent process for training/testing split with confidence intervals around AUC, accuracy, specificity.
